claude_result.result: {"answers":{"q1":"Under the current design the steward chooses the subsequent work, not the orchestrator and not the operator's instruction to the orchestrator. The accepted, current claim steward-next-work (sources: source-2) states the steward always chooses next work after a failed attempt, and it governs the operation choose-next-work. The necessary distinction is between deciding which subsequent work pursues the intention (choose-next-work, a steward decision) and the mechanical act of inserting or creating a record, which choose-next-work explicitly says is distinct. The orchestrator may end the failed attempt and return it to the steward, and may ask 'keep trying versus mark failed' (source-2, steward-next-work rationale), but selecting the replacement work belongs to the steward. The withdrawn claims replacement-exception and atomic-replacement, which would have let an operator-approved orchestrator replacement bypass the steward, are marked historical and revised by steward-next-work, so an operator telling the orchestrator to create replacement work does not shift the choice away from the steward. Also, per concern-persists, ending the failed attempt does not satisfy or withdraw the underlying intention, so the intention still needs steward-chosen work.","q2":"Yes. Two related withdrawn claims record an earlier policy: replacement-exception ('Operator-approved orchestrator replacement can bypass steward', source-1) and atomic-replacement ('Orchestrator replacement is atomic archive/add and does not wake steward until new work completes', sources source-1 and source-2). Rationale for the earlier policy: avoid a relay when the orchestrator already had the context (source-1; replacement-exception rationale). Why it changed: Blake later chose the simpler rule that the steward always chooses the work (source-2), preferring a single owner of the next-work choice and a clean responsibility boundary (steward-next-work rationale; replacement-exception rationale 'later rejected in favor of one owner of next-work choice'; atomic-replacement rationale 'retired when steward always choosing was selected'). The explicit relations confirm steward-next-work revises both replacement-exception and atomic-replacement. Both older claims have status withdrawn and review_state historical.","q3":"No, the current theory does not establish a requirement for operator permission every time. Settled (accepted, current): the steward always chooses next work after a failed attempt (steward-next-work, source-2); the orchestrator may end a failed attempt and return it to the steward (steward-next-work rationale); ending a failed attempt does not itself satisfy or withdraw the underlying intention (concern-persists, source-2). Open (status open, current): the question consultation asks whether the orchestrator must consult the operator before ending degraded work or may end autonomously within a configured threshold; its rationale notes that 'may ask' in source-2 does not establish mandatory consultation and that this is not settled by next-work ownership. Also open: cancellation, whether every arbitrary cancellation wakes the steward beyond the agreed failed terminal result (source-2). So consultation requirements and the scope of what wakes the steward remain undecided; the packet gives no threshold value or consultation rule.","q4":"Per source-3, only summaries of M1688 and M1689 are supplied, and the primary postmortems are unavailable in this fixture. What the material can establish: at the level of summary, M1688 describes a pattern of repeated useful reviews without an effective ruling, and M1689 describes planning a proposed solution instead of reassessing the original performance concern. These summaries are consistent with the design's motivation for a single owner of the next-work choice (steward-next-work) and for the claim that ending an attempt does not resolve the underlying concern (concern-persists), but no packet claim lists source-3 as a source, so the postmortems are not cited as evidence for any accepted claim. What it cannot establish: the specific details, causes, participants, timelines, or recommendations of the postmortems; whether either incident directly motivated the change from replacement-exception to steward-next-work (that change is attributed to source-1 and source-2, not source-3); and any resolution of the open questions consultation or cancellation. Any further characterization of M1688 or M1689 beyond the two summary sentences would be invention."}}
